entries.subject: Use abbreviations to speed up the NTT/INTT proofs (#325)
entries.message:
Use abbreviations to speed up the NTT/INTT proofs (#325)

This makes some changes to the NTT proofs and the underlying
infrastructure, in order to use abbreviations for large subterms. This
improves the runtimes of the x86 NTT/INTT proofs by a factor of
between 1.6 and 4.3 on my test machine, though the approach is
simple-minded and could probably be significantly improved. The two
main new functions used are:

 - ASM_CONGBOUND_RULE is a generalization of GEN_CONGBOUND_RULE to take
   an arbitrary environment of congruence+bound assumptions. This is more
   or less just exposing the internal function "rule" from GEN_CONGBOUND_RULE
   at the top level.

 - SIMD_SIMPLIFY_ABBREV_TAC is a variant of SIMD_SIMPLIFY_TAC that also
   introduces abbreviations for relevant subterms.

The overall structure of the proofs is similar, though in cases with
additional ad-hoc simplifications, steps need to be taken to apply them
also to the abbreviation assumptions.
entries.reason: Speeds x86 NTT/INTT HOL proofs through abbreviations.
entries.coverage: historical message/path screen; no source-matched HOL Light before/after check

entries.subject: AArch64/x86-64: Add persistent cosimulation protocol
entries.message:
AArch64/x86-64: Add persistent cosimulation protocol

Instruction cosimulation checks the HOL Light architecture model against
an external executor. A HOL worker generates an encoded instruction and
input state, sends them to the executor, and compares its output with
the model's result. Each worker currently executes one case through a
shell command:

```text
HOL worker -> temporary output file
           -> armsimulate/x86simulate
              -> preprocess -> assemble -> link -> execute
           -> parse the output file
```

The HOL-side drivers are `arm/proofs/simulator.ml` and
`x86/proofs/simulator.ml`. They generate the instruction and state,
start the executor, and compare its result with the HOL model. The
shared protocol client is implemented in `common/cosim.ml`.

The command-line simulators rebuild and start a temporary executable for
every case. The HOL drivers are also tied to shell argument quoting and
temporary output-file parsing. This repeats process and build startup
costs, and makes it difficult to substitute an emulator or another
instruction-execution transport.

Define version 1 of a line protocol over standard input and output:

```text
HOL worker <-> armsimulate-persistent/x86simulate-persistent
                         -> armsimulate/x86simulate
                            -> preprocess -> assemble -> link -> execute
```

The new wrappers keep the protocol connection open, translate each
request into the legacy command-line form, validate the returned state,
and report `OK`, `TRAP`, or `ERROR`. `READY` identifies the protocol,
architecture, and state size; `QUIT` ends the session.

Each `simulator.ml` selects a default executor command and an
environment variable that can replace it:

```text
S2N_BIGNUM_AARCH64_EXECUTOR
S2N_BIGNUM_X86_64_EXECUTOR
```

The override is a complete shell command, so it can add an emulator
prefix or select another protocol-speaking backend.

This separates case generation from instruction execution and provides
a transport boundary for emulators or other backends. Each request
still follows the historical per-case build path; reusing a compiled
runner is left to a later change.

Signed-off-by: Hanno Becker <beckphan@amazon.co.uk>
entries.reason: Keeps the cosimulation protocol process alive to avoid repeated startup costs.
entries.coverage: historical message/path screen; no source-matched HOL Light before/after check

entries.subject: Use native OCaml compiler to build & run proofs
entries.message:
Use native OCaml compiler to build & run proofs

This patch compiles proofs using native OCaml compiler, and updates
`make proofs` to run the newly created `*.native` executable files.

The new `tools/build-proof.sh` script builds a specific `.ml` proof file.
It inlines all loads/needs in the `.ml` file using HOL Light's
`inline_load.ml`.
Then, it collects all specifications in the original `.ml` file using already existing
`tools/collect-specs.sh`, and adds a print statement at the end of the
file, to make its standard output pass the proof checker script.
It also adds timer and prints the running time of the proof.
Then it is compiled with `ocamlopt.byte`.

Building all proofs can be done with `make build_proofs`. This uses a
lot of memory, so compared to the previous version `-j` number given to
`make` must be reduced.

This also makes the prerequisite lists tidier using the '*.native'
items. Each '.native' file is considered as depending on the '.o' file.
entries.reason: Builds and runs proofs with native OCaml to reduce proof runtime.
entries.coverage: historical message/path screen; no source-matched HOL Light before/after check

entries.message:
Add 4-way batch hybrid Keccak code based on mlkem-native

This adds a 4-way batch implementation of Keccak-f1600, taking a
100-element input/output array considered as four successive
independent Keccak states a[0..24], a[25..49], a[50..74], a[75..99];
the same Keccak-f1600 permutation is applied to each one. The code is
closely based on an mlkem-native original that mixes SIMD and scalar
operations:

      https://github.com/pq-code-package/mlkem-native/blob/main/mlkem/fips202/native/aarch64/src/keccak_f1600_x4_scalar_v84a_asm_hybrid_opt.S

The main change is the use of transpositions and plain load/store
in place of ld2/st2.

entries.subject: Optimize P-256 and P-384 modular tripling
entries.message:
Optimize P-256 and P-384 modular tripling

It seems to make them markedly more efficient doing the initial
3 * x operation via a double carry chain (adcx/adox) instead of
using the multiplier (mulx). There are a few other very minor
tweaks.
entries.reason: Replaces multiplier use with a faster double carry chain in modular tripling.
entries.coverage: historical message/path screen; no source-matched HOL Light before/after check

entries.subject: Add mlkem_keccak_f1600_alt using SHA3 instructions
entries.message:
Add mlkem_keccak_f1600_alt using SHA3 instructions

This adds another version of mlkem_keccak_f1600, using ARM sha3
instructions, which can sometimes be much faster than the scalar
approach on platforms that support them (e.g. on Apple M1).
This also represents a significant departure from s2n-bignum's
previous norms: it is the first piece of ARM code that will not
work on *every* 64-bit ARM machine.

The code is closely based on an original in mlkem-native

  https://github.com/pq-code-package/mlkem-native/blob/main/mlkem/fips202/native/aarch64/src/keccak_f1600_x1_v84a_asm_clean.S

with some minor changes to make it fit the s2n-bignum model better.
entries.reason: Adds a SHA3-instruction Keccak alternative for faster supported ARM CPUs.
entries.coverage: historical message/path screen; no source-matched HOL Light before/after check

entries.subject: Slightly improve x86 P-256 and P-384 Montgomery operations
entries.message:
Slightly improve x86 P-256 and P-384 Montgomery operations

This commit makes various minor local improvements such as the use of
32-bit operations where possible (which generally reduces code size),
and generates some big constants avoiding the use of 64-bit immediate
moves. The Montgomery multiplies also do some of the top parts of
carry chains in a slightly more efficient way; this is the only case
where the actual dataflow changes, and even so the same proofs still
work modulo the instruction offsets and code size changes. Code size
is reduced for sure, and there seems to be some slight (maybe 1-3%?)
efficiency gain on both Xeon and EPYC. This commit also makes a couple
of tweaks to simulation in order to handle 32-bit ADC more nicely and
to trivialize the zero-extension of single-bit values "word(bitval b)".
entries.reason: Reduces code size and carry-chain work in P-256/P-384 Montgomery operations.
entries.coverage: historical message/path screen; no source-matched HOL Light before/after check

entries.subject: Slightly optimize curve25519 field multiplication and squaring
entries.message:
Slightly optimize curve25519 field multiplication and squaring

Both bignum_mul_p25519 and bignum_sqr_p25519 in effect reduce
a double-length 2^256 * h + l to congruent 38 * h + l and then
further reduce based on a quotient estimate from the latter.
The new versions slightly reduce dependent latencies and/or
number of instructions by forming the quotient estimate before
the full computation of 38 * h + l and feeding the subsequent
correction in earlier as a result.
entries.reason: Reduces dependent latency and instruction count in curve25519 multiplication and squaring.
entries.coverage: historical message/path screen; no source-matched HOL Light before/after check
